rows.stem: In its extended 'beads-on-string' form of chromatin, the 'beads' in the string represent :
rows.solution: In the nucleus the negatively charged DNA is wrapped around a positively charged **histone octamer** (eight histone molecules), forming a unit called the **nucleosome**; a typical nucleosome holds about 200 bp of DNA. Repeating nucleosomes form the chromatin thread, which under the electron microscope looks like **beads on a string**: the nucleosomes are the beads and the **linker DNA** joining them is the string. So the answer is option (C) Nucleosomes.

rows.stem:
Given below are a few statements with reference to the accessory ducts of the human male reproductive system :
(i) The seminiferous tubules of the testes open into rete testis then into the vas deferens.
(ii) The vasa efferentia leave the testes and open into the epididymis.
(iii) The epididymis leads to vas deferens that ascends into the abdomen.
(iv) The vas deferens receives a duct from the prostrate gland and opens into the urethra as ejaculatory duct.
(v) The urethra originates from the urinary bladder and extends through the penis to its external opening, urethral meatus.
Choose the option with all true statements from the given options :
rows.solution:
Checking each statement against the path sperms take out of the testis:
- (i) is false: the seminiferous tubules open into the vas deferens only after passing through the rete testis, the **vasa efferentia** and the **epididymis**, not directly from the rete testis.
- (ii) is true: the vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis on its posterior surface.
- (iii) is true: the epididymis leads to the vas deferens, which ascends into the abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder.
- (iv) is false: the vas deferens receives a duct from the **seminal vesicle** (not the prostate gland, printed here as "prostrate") and opens into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct.
- (v) is true: the urethra originates from the urinary bladder and extends through the penis to its external opening, the urethral meatus.

So the true statements are (ii), (iii) and (v). So the answer is option (B) (ii), (iii), (v).

rows.stem: The substrate used during DNA replication by the enzyme DNA-dependent DNA polymerase is :
rows.solution: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase uses a DNA template to polymerise a large number of nucleotides. Its substrates are the **deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates** (dATP, dGTP, dCTP, dTTP), which serve a dual purpose: they are the building blocks of the new strand, and the energy released on removing two of their phosphates drives the polymerisation reaction. So the answer is option (B) Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate.

rows.stem:
In the given pedigree chart, a cross between a normal couple resulted in a son who was haemophilic and a normal daughter. In course of time, when the daughter was married to a normal man, to their surprise the grandson was also haemophilic.
Choose the option that indicates the correct inheritance of trait in the above pedigree chart :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE:a pedigree: an unshaded square and an unshaded circle joined as a couple, with two children, a shaded square (son) and an unshaded circle (daughter); the daughter is joined to an unshaded square and their child is a shaded square. The stem states every relationship and phenotype the chart shows, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
- Both parents are normal but their son is affected, so the trait is **recessive**: the parents carry the allele without showing it.
- Only males are affected, and the trait passes from an unaffected mother to her son and then through an unaffected daughter (a carrier) to her son, the grandson. This criss-cross passage through carrier females is typical of an allele on the **X chromosome**.
- Haemophilia is indeed a sex-linked recessive disorder: a carrier mother \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{X}\) passes \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) to half her sons, who are haemophilic because a male has only one X chromosome. The daughter received \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) from her mother and passed it to her own son.

So the answer is option (D) Sex-linked recessive trait.

rows.stem: In which of the following human diseases does the body's self-defence mechanism attack self-cells ?
rows.solution: Sometimes, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body's defence mechanism attacks its own cells. This damages the body and is called **autoimmune disease**; **rheumatoid arthritis** is an example. Thalassemia and phenylketonuria are Mendelian (genetic) disorders, and filariasis is an infection caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria. So the answer is option (D) Rheumatoid arthritis.

rows.stem:
Select the statements that are true for a typical dicotyledonous embryo from the given options.
(i) It consists of an embryonal axis and scutellum.
(ii) The portion of embryonal axis above the level of cotyledon is epicotyl.
(iii) The portion of embryonal axis below the level of cotyledon is coleorhiza.
(iv) The lower end of the embryo has radicle covered with a root cap.
Choose the correct answer :
rows.solution:
A typical dicot embryo has an embryonal axis and **two cotyledons**.
- (i) is false: the scutellum is the single cotyledon of a monocot (grass) embryo, not of a dicot embryo.
- (ii) is true: the portion of the embryonal axis above the level of the cotyledons is the **epicotyl**, which ends in the plumule (stem tip).
- (iii) is false: the portion below the level of the cotyledons is the **hypocotyl**; the coleorhiza is the sheath round the radicle in a monocot embryo.
- (iv) is true: the hypocotyl ends at its lower end in the **radicle** (root tip), covered with a root cap.

So the answer is option (D) (ii) and (iv).

rows.stem: About 15 mya during human evolution, the primates which used to walk like gorillas and chimpanzees were :
rows.solution: About 15 mya, primates called **Dryopithecus** and **Ramapithecus** were existing. They were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Ramapithecus was more man-like while Dryopithecus was more ape-like. The Australopithecines appeared much later (about 2 mya), Homo habilis and Homo erectus later still, and the Neanderthal man and Homo sapiens are recent. So the answer is option (B) Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus.

rows.stem:
Use the given information to select the amino acid attached to the 3' end of tRNA during the process of translation, if the coding strand of the structural gene being transcribed has the nucleotide sequence TAC.
Codons for the amino acids :
AUC – Isoleucine
AUG – Methionine
UAC – Tyrosine
GUA – Valine
rows.solution:
The mRNA has the same sequence as the **coding strand** of the gene, with uracil in place of thymine.
- Coding strand: TAC, so the mRNA codon is **UAC**.
- From the given codons, UAC codes for **tyrosine**.

During translation the tRNA whose anticodon (AUG) pairs with the codon UAC carries tyrosine attached to its 3' end. So the answer is option (C) Tyrosine.

rows.stem: The technique for the early detection of a disease based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction is :
rows.solution: **ELISA** (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay) is based on the principle of **antigen-antibody interaction**. Infection by a pathogen can be detected by the presence of its antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen, which allows early diagnosis. PCR and RNAi work on nucleic acids, and ESTs are expressed sequence tags of genome sequencing. So the answer is option (D) ELISA.

rows.stem: The correct depiction of the experiment performed by Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl to prove that DNA replicates semi-conservatively on separation of DNA by centrifugation after 40 minutes is :

options.label: A
options.text: Figure (A) as printed: a tube with two dark bands, about one-quarter and three-fifths of the way from the capped end to the rounded end

options.label: B
options.text: Figure (B) as printed: a tube with one dark band at the rounded end

options.label: C
options.text: Figure (C) as printed: a tube with two dark bands, one next to the capped end and one at the rounded end

options.label: D
options.text: Figure (D) as printed: a tube with one dark band about three-fifths of the way from the capped end to the rounded end

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:all four options are drawn centrifuge tubes lying on their side, capped end at the left and rounded closed end at the right, each carrying one or two dark DNA bands. The option texts say only where each band sits along the tube; which DNA density each position stands for is what the question tests, so it is not named. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in a medium with \(^{15}\text{N}\) as the only nitrogen source, so its DNA became heavy, and then transferred the cells to a medium with normal \(^{14}\text{N}\). E. coli divides every 20 minutes, and the DNA was separated by density in a caesium chloride gradient.
- At 0 minutes all the DNA is heavy (\(^{15}\text{N}\) \(^{15}\text{N}\)): one band at the heavy end of the tube.
- After 20 minutes (one generation) all the DNA is **hybrid** (\(^{15}\text{N}\) \(^{14}\text{N}\)): one band at an intermediate density.
- After **40 minutes** (two generations) there are **equal amounts of hybrid DNA and light DNA** (\(^{14}\text{N}\) \(^{14}\text{N}\)): two bands, one at the intermediate position and one at the lighter position, nearer the top of the tube.

In the drawings the rounded closed end is the bottom of the tube, where the heaviest DNA settles. The single band three-fifths of the way along is the 20-minute hybrid band; the tube that shows that band together with a second band nearer the capped (top) end is the 40-minute result. A single band at the closed end is the starting heavy DNA, and a band at each end would mean the heavy parental duplex had survived intact, which is the conservative pattern the experiment ruled out. So the answer is option (A), the tube with two bands, one at the hybrid position and one nearer the top.

rows.stem: Bioactive molecule Cyclosporin A used for human welfare is derived from :
rows.solution: **Cyclosporin A**, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients, is produced by the fungus **Trichoderma polysporum**. Propionibacterium shermanii (printed here as 'sharmanii') makes the large holes in Swiss cheese, Monascus purpureus yields the blood-cholesterol lowering statins, and Aspergillus niger produces citric acid. So the answer is option (C) Trichoderma polysporum.

rows.stem: In a pea plant (Pisum sativum) inflated pod shape is dominant over constricted pod shape. The expected ratio of phenotypes of the offspring in a cross between both the parents with heterozygous inflated pod shape will be :
rows.solution:
Let I be the allele for inflated pods (dominant) and i the allele for constricted pods. Both parents are heterozygous, Ii.
- Ii \(\times\) Ii gives II : Ii : ii in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
- II and Ii both have inflated pods, and only ii has constricted pods.

So the phenotypic ratio is 3 inflated : 1 constricted. So the answer is option (D) 3 : 1.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The meristems are grown 'in vitro' to obtain virus-free plants from an infected plant.
Reason (R) : If the plant is infected with a virus, the roots and the stems are free of virus.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: virus-free plants are obtained from an infected plant by removing its **meristem** and growing it in vitro (tissue culture). The Reason is false: even if a plant is infected with a virus, it is the **meristem (apical and axillary)** that is free of virus, not the roots and the stems, which carry the virus. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A person infected with malaria suffers from chill and high fever, recurring every three or four days.
Reason (R) : The parasite attacks the RBC resulting in their rupture and release of haemozoin.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: a person with malaria suffers from chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. The Reason is also true and explains it: Plasmodium reproduces asexually in the red blood cells, **bursting the RBCs** and releasing a toxic substance, **haemozoin**, which is responsible for the chill and high fever. The fever recurs with each new round of RBC rupture. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : 'Saheli', an oral contraceptive inhibits ovulation and increases phagocytosis of sperms.
Reason (R) : It is a non-steroidal preparation.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is false: oral pills inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter the quality of cervical mucus, but **increasing the phagocytosis of sperms** within the uterus is the action of intra uterine devices (IUDs), not of a pill. The Reason is true: Saheli, the once-a-week pill developed at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow, contains a **non-steroidal preparation**. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : ABO blood grouping in humans is an example of multiple allelism.
Reason (R) : More than two genes in a population govern the same character in ABO blood grouping in humans.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: ABO blood grouping is a good example of **multiple alleles**. The Reason is false: the ABO blood group is controlled by a **single gene**, I, which has three alleles, \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i. Multiple allelism means more than two **alleles of one gene** govern the same character in a population; it does not mean more than two genes, and since a person is diploid, each individual carries only two of the three alleles. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem: Explain how the immunity of a person is affected if there is atrophy (degeneration) of the thymus gland at an early stage of life.
rows.solution:
- The thymus is a **primary lymphoid organ** where immature lymphocytes differentiate into **antigen-sensitive T-lymphocytes**. It is quite large at birth and gradually reduces in size with age, so its role is greatest in early life.
- If the thymus degenerates at an early stage, the development and maturation of T-lymphocytes does not take place.
- The **immunity of the person will decrease**: cell-mediated immunity, which depends on T-lymphocytes, is lost, and the antibody (humoral) response is also weakened because helper T-cells are needed to help B-cells produce antibodies. The person becomes highly prone to infections.

rows.stem:
(i) What are interferons ? Explain their role in providing immunity to a person.
(ii) Which category of innate immunity defence barrier can interferons be classified into ?
rows.solution:
(i) **Interferons** are proteins secreted by **virus-infected cells**. They protect the **non-infected cells from further viral infection**, so they limit the spread of the virus in the body.

(ii) Interferons belong to the **cytokine barriers** of innate immunity.

rows.stem:
Assume that the given mRNA (start site is not depicted) is theoretically translated in two reading frames.
(a) Translation starting from the first nucleotide (Reading frame 1)
(b) Translation starting from the second nucleotide (Reading frame 2)
Frame 1
5' – CUCGCUUGCCGAUCAAGGGUUA – 3'
Frame 2
5' – GUGGCACUCAGUCCUUAAUGGCG – 3'
Answer the following question :
How many amino acids will be specified in case (a) and case (b) on translation ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
The genetic code is a **triplet**: three adjacent nucleotides form one codon, which specifies one amino acid, and the code is read without overlaps or gaps. A codon that is not one of the stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) specifies an amino acid, and a leftover of fewer than three bases specifies nothing. The paper prints a separate sequence for each frame; each is read as printed.

(a) **Reading frame 1**, from the first nucleotide of 5' – CUCGCUUGCCGAUCAAGGGUUA – 3':
CUC GCU UGC CGA UCA AGG GUU, with A left over.
That is 7 codons and none is a stop codon, so **7 amino acids** are specified.

(b) **Reading frame 2**, from the second nucleotide of 5' – GUGGCACUCAGUCCUUAAUGGCG – 3' (the first G is skipped):
UGG CAC UCA GUC CUU AAU GGC, with G left over.
Again 7 codons and none is a stop codon, so **7 amino acids** are specified.

Shifting the start by one base regroups every triplet, which is why a reading frame matters: had the second sequence been read from its first nucleotide, its sixth codon would be UAA, a stop codon, and only 5 amino acids would be specified.

rows.stem: Explain what is meant by the term MTP. What was the main reason to legalize MTP by the Government of India ?
rows.solution:
- **MTP** (medical termination of pregnancy) is the intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term.
- The Government of India legalised MTP (in 1971, with strict conditions to avoid its misuse) so that **unwanted pregnancies** could be got rid of safely: those due to casual unprotected intercourse, failure of the contraceptive used during coitus, or rape, and those where continuing the pregnancy could be **harmful or even fatal to the mother, the foetus or both**.

The restrictions also help to check indiscriminate and illegal female foeticide, and the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017 aims to reduce the incidence of illegal abortion and the maternal deaths it causes.

rows.stem: Name any two STIs which might occur in a human female. State its two early symptoms.
rows.solution:
- **Two STIs** (any two): gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, HIV leading to AIDS.
- **Two early symptoms** (any two): itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings in the genital region. Early symptoms are often minor, and in females these infections are frequently asymptomatic, so they may remain undetected for long.

rows.stem:
The basic scheme of the essential steps involved in the process of recombinant DNA technology is summarized below in the form of a flow diagram. Study the given flow diagram and answer the questions that follow.
Step-1 Vector DNA (cut using Restriction Enzyme EcoR I) + Alien DNA (cut using Restriction Enzyme EcoR I)
\(\downarrow\) Enzyme A
Step-2 Recombinant DNA molecule
\(\downarrow\)
Step-3 Transfer of recombinant DNA molecule in E. coli (Host)
\(\downarrow\)
Step-4 Replication of recombinant DNA molecule in E. coli
(a) Name the enzyme used in Step-1 to join the cut plasmid and alien DNA.
(b) State the technical term used for Step-3.
(c) Justify the use of same Restriction Enzyme EcoR I to cut both the vector DNA and the alien DNA.
rows.solution:
(a) **DNA ligase** (enzyme A) joins the cut plasmid (vector DNA) and the alien DNA, sealing the sugar-phosphate backbones to form the recombinant DNA molecule.

(b) Step 3, introducing the recombinant DNA into the host E. coli, is called **transformation**.

(c) The same restriction enzyme, EcoR I, recognises the same palindromic sequence (5' GAATTC 3') in both DNAs and cuts each of them between G and A on both strands, leaving the **same kind of sticky ends**, single-stranded overhangs that are **complementary** to each other. The sticky end of the vector therefore pairs with the sticky end of the alien DNA by hydrogen bonds, and DNA ligase can then join them. DNAs cut with different enzymes would carry ends that do not match.

rows.stem: Explain how the interaction between sea anemone and clownfish is one of the best examples of commensalism in nature.
rows.solution:
Commensalism is an interaction in which one species benefits and the other is **neither harmed nor benefited**.
- The **clownfish** lives among the **stinging tentacles** of the sea anemone and gets **protection from predators**, which stay away from the stinging tentacles. So the clownfish benefits.
- The **sea anemone** neither derives any benefit from the clownfish nor gets harmed by it.

So the clownfish benefits while the sea anemone is unaffected, which is exactly commensalism (+, 0).

rows.stem: Correctly depict (also indicate the trophic level) and describe the ecological pyramid of biomass in sea with 40 standing crop of phytoplankton supporting 90 standing crop of zooplankton which further supports 120 small fishes.
Explain the process of formation of placenta in a human female after the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium of the uterus.
rows.solution:
- After **implantation**, finger-like projections called **chorionic villi** appear on the **trophoblast**.
- The chorionic villi are surrounded by the **uterine tissue and maternal blood**.
- The chorionic villi and the uterine tissue become **interdigitated** with each other and jointly form a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo (foetus) and the maternal body, called the **placenta**.
- The placenta is connected to the embryo through the **umbilical cord**, which helps in the transport of substances to and from the embryo.

Through the placenta the embryo receives oxygen and nutrients and gets rid of carbon dioxide and excretory wastes. The placenta also acts as an endocrine tissue, producing hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.

rows.stem:
Gregor Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments in garden pea for seven years and proposed the law of inheritance.
(a) Why was he successful in his hybridisation experiments ? Give two reasons.
(b) State the law of independent assortment as proposed by Mendel after his dihybrid crosses.

Study the given below single strand of deoxyribonucleic acid depicted in the form of a "stick" diagram with 5' – 3' end directionality, sugars as vertical lines and bases as single letter abbreviations and answer the questions that follow.
(a) Name the covalent bonds depicted as (a) and (b) in the form of slanting lines in the diagram.
(b) How many purines are present in the given "stick" diagram ?
(c) Draw the chemical structure of the given polynucleotide chain of DNA.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a 'stick' diagram of a three-nucleotide strand: three vertical sugar lines, each topped by a boxed base letter; a circled P at the left joined by a slanting line marked (a) to the 5' foot of the first sugar; slanting lines from the 3' position of each sugar to the 5' foot of the next, one of them marked (b); and a circled OH at the 3' end of the last sugar. The three base letters decide (b) and (c), so they are withheld here. Page idx 18.

rows.stem: Explain the biological treatment of primary effluent when passed into the large aeration tanks in a sewage treatment plant (STP).

Given below is a flower with its characteristic features specialised for the most common type of abiotic pollination.
Answer the following questions based on the above diagram :
(a) Name the mode of abiotic pollination that will be adopted by the given plant species in the above picture.
(b) State the need of exposed large feathery stigmas for the flower.
(c) What will be the two important adaptations in the pollen grains of the flowers pollinated by the above mode of pollination ?
(d) What could be the probable reason for the petals being small and non-green ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE:a coloured drawing of a small flower with long dangling stamens and large feathery stigmas held well out of the flower, labelled 'Feathery stigma', 'Versatile Anther', 'Ovary' and 'Petals'. The stem already says the flower is specialised for the most common type of abiotic pollination and names its feathery stigmas, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(a) The flower is adapted for **wind pollination (anemophily)**, the most common type of abiotic pollination.

(b) The large, exposed, **feathery stigmas** are needed to **trap the air-borne pollen grains** carried by the wind.

(c) Two adaptations of the pollen grains: they are **light and non-sticky**, so they can be easily transported by wind currents. They are also produced in very large numbers.

(d) The petals are small and non-green because a wind-pollinated flower **need not attract insects, birds or bats**, so there is no advantage in large, colourful petals; small petals also do not obstruct the **flow of wind** to the well-exposed stamens and stigmas.

rows.stem:
According to a recent wildlife report, the biggest threat to the tiger's survival in Mudumalai Tiger Reserve (MTR) was found to be a small, beautiful flower, Lantana camara, a tropical American shrub, that invaded 40% of India's tiger range. Tamil Nadu department's Lantana weed eradication drive helped to restore the dying MTR thereby also reducing human-wildlife conflicts. MTR is home to 25 species of grasses and legumes.
Answer the given questions based on the information given above.
(a) Explain how did the removal of Lantana help in restoring the dying Mudumalai Tiger Reserve.
(b) Why is the invasion of Lantana camara a cause of concern in MTR.
rows.solution:
(a)
- Lantana camara is an invasive alien weed that spreads aggressively and does not allow native plants, such as the grasses and legumes of the reserve, to grow in its surroundings.
- **Removal of Lantana** allows these native grasses and legumes to grow back, so more food is available for **herbivores**, and the herbivore population increases.
- With more prey (herbivores) available, the **tiger population** is restored, and tigers no longer need to stray out of the reserve in search of prey, which also reduces human-wildlife conflicts.

(b) Lantana camara is an **alien species invasion**, one of the major causes of loss of biodiversity. Being invasive, it does not allow other plants to grow around it, which **decreases the herbivore population**, and this in turn can cause a **decline in the tiger population** of the reserve.

rows.stem: Enlist one advantage and two disadvantages of green revolution.

To which category of evolution (Divergent or Convergent) do the following evolutionary relationships belong to :
(i) Humans and Macaque
(ii) Humans and Frog
rows.context:
The most convincing evidence to trace evolutionary relationships between humans and different groups of animals come from the basic similarities seen at the molecular level. Study the table given below that depicts the number of amino acid differences between the haemoglobin polypeptide of few animals with that of humans and answer the questions that follow.
| S.No. | Animal | No. of amino acid differences in haemoglobin with that of humans |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Macaque | 08 |
| 2. | Dog | 32 |
| 3. | Bird | 45 |
| 4. | Frog | 67 |
| 5. | Lamprey | 125 |
rows.solution:
Both relationships belong to **divergent evolution**:
- (i) Humans and macaque: divergent evolution.
- (ii) Humans and frog: divergent evolution.

Humans, macaques and frogs all descended from a common ancestor and then diverged into different forms, so their haemoglobin is a homologous molecule that has gradually accumulated differences. Convergent evolution is the opposite case, in which unrelated groups evolve similar features for a similar function.

rows.stem: What do the biochemical similarities in haemoglobin suggest about the evolutionary relationship between humans, frog and lamprey ?
rows.context:
The most convincing evidence to trace evolutionary relationships between humans and different groups of animals come from the basic similarities seen at the molecular level. Study the table given below that depicts the number of amino acid differences between the haemoglobin polypeptide of few animals with that of humans and answer the questions that follow.
| S.No. | Animal | No. of amino acid differences in haemoglobin with that of humans |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Macaque | 08 |
| 2. | Dog | 32 |
| 3. | Bird | 45 |
| 4. | Frog | 67 |
| 5. | Lamprey | 125 |
rows.solution: The biochemical similarities in haemoglobin suggest **common ancestry**: humans, frog and lamprey all share a common ancestor. The number of amino acid differences reflects how closely they are related. Humans and frog (67 differences) share a more recent common ancestor than humans and lamprey (125 differences), so the lamprey is the most distantly related of the three.

rows.stem: Which one of the two – lampreys' or macaques' evolution is more closely related to humans and why ?
rows.context:
The most convincing evidence to trace evolutionary relationships between humans and different groups of animals come from the basic similarities seen at the molecular level. Study the table given below that depicts the number of amino acid differences between the haemoglobin polypeptide of few animals with that of humans and answer the questions that follow.
| S.No. | Animal | No. of amino acid differences in haemoglobin with that of humans |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Macaque | 08 |
| 2. | Dog | 32 |
| 3. | Bird | 45 |
| 4. | Frog | 67 |
| 5. | Lamprey | 125 |
rows.solution: The **macaque** is more closely related to humans than the lamprey, because the number of amino acid differences between the haemoglobin of humans and macaque is much smaller (8) than between humans and lamprey (125). Humans and macaques therefore have more biochemical similarity in the structure of haemoglobin, which shows a more recent common ancestor.

rows.stem: Why are people taking opioids more prone to liver diseases attributed to Hepatitis B ?
rows.context:
Deaths related to the use of drugs were estimated at about 5,00,000 in 2019, \(17{\cdot}5\) percent more than in 2009. Liver diseases attributed to Hepatitis B are a major cause of drug-related deaths, according to UNODC, accounting for more than half of the total number of deaths attributed to the use of drugs. Drug overdoses account for a quarter of drug-related deaths.
Opioids contribute to account for the most severe drug-related harm, including fatal overdoses, when used non-medically. At the global level, two-third of direct drug-related deaths are due to opioids, and in some sub-regions the proportion can be as high as three-quarters of such deaths.
rows.solution: Opioids such as heroin are generally taken **intravenously**, directly into a vein using a needle and syringe. The use of **contaminated (shared) needles and syringes** transmits the hepatitis B virus, which infects the liver, so people taking opioids this way are much more likely to get liver diseases attributed to hepatitis B.

rows.stem: What is meant by direct drug-related disease ?
rows.context:
Deaths related to the use of drugs were estimated at about 5,00,000 in 2019, \(17{\cdot}5\) percent more than in 2009. Liver diseases attributed to Hepatitis B are a major cause of drug-related deaths, according to UNODC, accounting for more than half of the total number of deaths attributed to the use of drugs. Drug overdoses account for a quarter of drug-related deaths.
Opioids contribute to account for the most severe drug-related harm, including fatal overdoses, when used non-medically. At the global level, two-third of direct drug-related deaths are due to opioids, and in some sub-regions the proportion can be as high as three-quarters of such deaths.
rows.solution: A direct drug-related disease (or death) is one caused **directly by the drug itself**, mainly by an **overdose**, as in a fatal overdose of opioids. It differs from an indirect one, such as a liver disease from a hepatitis B infection picked up through a shared needle, which the drug only makes more likely.

rows.stem:
(i) Explain how does double fertilisation take place in a flowering plant.
(ii) Write the fate of the products of double fertilization in these plants.
rows.solution:
(i) **Double fertilisation**
- The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and then enters **one of the synergids** through the filiform apparatus.
- It releases the **two male gametes** into the cytoplasm of the synergid.
- One male gamete moves towards the **egg cell** and fuses with its nucleus, completing **syngamy**; this forms a diploid cell, the **zygote**.
- The other male gamete moves towards the **two polar nuclei** in the central cell and fuses with them to produce a triploid **primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**. As this involves the fusion of three haploid nuclei it is called **triple fusion**, and the central cell becomes the **primary endosperm cell (PEC)**.

Since two types of fusion, syngamy and triple fusion, take place in one embryo sac, the phenomenon is called double fertilisation.

(ii) **Fate of the products**
- The **primary endosperm cell (PEC)** develops into the **endosperm**, a triploid tissue that nourishes the developing embryo.
- The **zygote** develops into the **embryo**.

Following double fertilisation, the ovules mature into seeds and the ovary develops into the fruit.

rows.stem:
(i) Explain the structure of testicular lobules in human male reproductive system. Name the two types of cells present in the seminiferous tubules and state their role.
(ii) Describe the role of hypothalamic hormone GnRH in spermatogenesis.
rows.solution:
(i)
- Each testis has about 250 compartments called **testicular lobules**. Each lobule contains **one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules**, in which sperms are produced.
- Each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by two types of cells:
  - **male germ cells (spermatogonia)**, which undergo meiotic divisions finally leading to **sperm formation**;
  - **Sertoli cells**, which provide **nutrition to the germ cells**.
- The regions outside the seminiferous tubules, the interstitial spaces, contain small blood vessels and Leydig cells, which secrete androgens.

(ii) **Role of GnRH**
- Spermatogenesis starts at puberty because of a significant increase in the secretion of **gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)** by the hypothalamus.
- GnRH acts on the **anterior pituitary gland** and stimulates the secretion of two gonadotropins, **luteinising hormone (LH)** and **follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)**.
- LH acts on the Leydig cells and stimulates the synthesis and secretion of androgens, which in turn stimulate spermatogenesis.
- FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates the secretion of some factors that help in spermiogenesis.

rows.stem: Name and explain the biotechnological strategy wherein the infection by the nematode Meloidegyne incognitia can be prevented using Agrobacterium vectors in the roots of tobacco plant by RNA interference.
rows.solution:
The strategy is **RNA interference (RNAi)**. RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence: a specific mRNA is silenced by a complementary double-stranded RNA molecule that binds to it and prevents its translation.

The steps used to protect tobacco plants from the nematode Meloidogyne incognita (printed here as 'Meloidegyne incognitia'), which infects their roots and causes a great reduction in yield:
- Using **Agrobacterium vectors**, **nematode-specific genes** were introduced into the host (tobacco) plants.
- The DNA was introduced so that it produced **both sense and anti-sense RNA** in the host cells.
- The two RNAs, being complementary to each other, formed a **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)**.
- This dsRNA initiated RNAi and thus **silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode**.

Consequently the parasite could not survive in a transgenic host expressing the specific interfering RNA, and the transgenic plant got protected from the parasite.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem: Explain the amplification of gene of interest using the technique of Polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
rows.solution:
**Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)** makes multiple copies of the gene of interest in vitro, using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of the DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase. Each cycle has three steps:
- **Denaturation**: the double-stranded DNA is subjected to a high temperature, so the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous bases break and the two strands separate.
- **Annealing**: the two sets of primers, which are complementary to the template strands, attach to the 3' ends of the region to be amplified on both template strands.
- **Extension**: the thermostable **Taq polymerase** (isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it remains active during the high temperature of denaturation) extends the primers, using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as the template, forming new strands.

The cycle is repeated many times (about 30), and the DNA segment is amplified to approximately **1 billion times**, that is, 1 billion copies are made. The steps may also be shown as a diagram: the double-stranded DNA with the region to be amplified, heat separating the strands, primers annealing at the 3' ends, Taq polymerase with deoxynucleotides extending them, and 30 cycles giving the amplified DNA.

rows.stem:
(i) Describe the population growth curve applicable in a population of any species in nature that has limited resources at its disposal.
(ii) Give the equation of this growth curve.
(iii) Name the growth curve and depict a graphical plot for this type of population growth.
rows.solution:
(i) In nature a population has **limited resources** at its disposal, so sooner or later competition among individuals for these resources becomes fierce and only the fittest survive and reproduce. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows:
- initially a **lag phase**,
- followed by phases of **acceleration** and **deceleration**,
- and finally an **asymptote**, when the population density reaches the **carrying capacity (K)**, the maximum population the habitat can support.

(ii) The equation of this growth is
\(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K - N}{K}\right)\)
where N is the population density at time t, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K is the carrying capacity.

(iii) It is the **logistic (Verhulst-Pearl logistic) growth curve**, also called the sigmoid or **S-shaped** curve. The graph plots population density (N) on the y-axis against time (t) on the x-axis: the curve rises slowly at first, then steeply, then more slowly, and levels off along a dashed horizontal line marked K, the carrying capacity. Logistic growth is considered the more realistic model, since no population has unlimited resources.

rows.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
rows.stem:
(i) Explain the Species-Area relationship within a natural forest and also predict the nature of graph when species richness is plotted against the area for a wide variety of taxa.
(ii) Depict the graphical relationship between species richness and area.
(iii) Give the equation of the Species-Area relationship for a wide variety of taxa on a logarithmic scale.
rows.solution:
(i) Alexander von Humboldt observed that **within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit**; so a larger area of a natural forest holds more species, but each further increase in area adds fewer new species. For a wide variety of taxa (angiosperm plants, birds, bats, freshwater fishes) the relation between species richness and area turns out to be a **rectangular hyperbola**.

(ii) The graph plots species richness on the y-axis against area on the x-axis: the curve rises steeply at first and then flattens out, a rectangular hyperbola. On a logarithmic scale (log-log axes) the same relationship is a **straight line**. Either graph is accepted.

(iii) On a logarithmic scale the relationship is a straight line described by
\(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\)
(the same as \(S = CA^{Z}\)), where S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope of the line (the regression coefficient) and C is the Y-intercept. The value of Z generally lies between 0.1 and 0.2, whatever the taxonomic group or region, but for very large areas such as whole continents the line becomes much steeper, with Z between 0.6 and 1.2.
